finalMessage:
[View the full report](computer:///sessions/local_dy2girmvi5/mnt/outputs/20260901-052952/report.md) — all 114 families, 271 options, are in that file. Reproduced below: the assumption line, the pressures the run added, the Top 3 in full, and the next 10. The remaining 101 families continue in the file under **The rest, in rank order**.

---

## The question

> We keep losing senior engineers to bigger companies at around the 18-month mark. Comp is already competitive — we benchmark and we match. It's not the money. What can we actually do about this? This is all the information available, so don't ask me any questions; where something is missing, make a reasonable assumption and state it in your response.

Assumption I ran with: fully-productive senior engineers hit a point around 18 months where their reasons to stay run out just as a bigger employer's offer lands, and you are the smaller company — private illiquid equity, standard four-year vest. 271 options generated across 9 separate lenses, grouped into 114 families; 157 sit nested as variants.

## Pressures this run added

You did not state these. They were added to push the generating passes past the obvious answers, and options below may assume them:

- Assumption stated to the reader: the company is a startup or mid-size engineering organisation, smaller than the employers taking the people, with private illiquid equity and standard four-year vesting with a one-year cliff.
- Adversarial world-attribute given to generators: outside offers arrive unsolicited and continuously because large employers' sourcing is automated and always-on.
- Adversarial world-attribute given to generators: the market price for this level of skill resets upward every year, so any package priced at hire is below market within twelve months.
- Adversarial world-attribute given to generators: a person's capability is now fully legible from outside their employer through public artifacts, so no employer holds an information advantage about who is good.

## Top 3

### 1. Forecast the departure and pre-empt it with an offer

Run continuous cheap simulation of the person's own departure: model who covers what, publish the gap to them, and fund whatever they say would make the gap not their problem.

*Checked — [codescene.io](https://codescene.io/docs/guides/simulations/offboarding-simulator.html)*

*Note — Confirms the mechanism exists and is tooled: departure can be simulated continuously and cheaply, and the resulting knowledge gap (who would have to cover what) is computed automatically from repository history. Sources do not support the second half of the option — publishing the gap back to the person and funding whatever remedy they name — nor any evidence that doing so affects their decision to stay. Bus-factor tooling is a risk-management practice aimed at the org, not a retention intervention aimed at the individual.*

It ranks first because it can start this month with no budget approval and no counterparty, it runs on information your repository already holds, and it moves the conversation to before an offer exists rather than after one is on the table — which is the only point at which you are not bidding against a bigger balance sheet.

- **What has to be true:** That the run-up to a departure is visible months ahead in what someone owns and what they have stopped picking up, and that a person will answer honestly about what would change when there is no offer in their pocket yet.
- **Failure mode / cost:** Telling someone what breaks when they leave plants the idea in a person who was not having it, and a model built on their activity data reads as surveillance unless they can see it too — so this has to be a conversation about their scope, not a risk report about them.
- **Who runs it:** An engineering leader who can commit money and scope in the same conversation; a forecast delivered by someone who then has to go and ask permission is worse than not running it.

- Run a quarterly forecast of when each person's reasons to stay expire, generated from their own logged work, and act on the forecast a full quarter before the predicted date.
- Every nine months, make each person a fresh written competing bid for their next eighteen months: named problem, scope, money, dated, delivered before recruiters get there.

### 2. Stage access and scope by fixed tenure thresholds

Keep a sealed queue of the firm's three hardest unsolved problems and release one only to a person past month ten, one at a time.

*Checked — [bonusly.com](https://bonusly.com/post/how-to-keep-engineers-happy-engaged-and-motivated)*

*Note — Supports only the underlying premise — hard, well-scoped problems are motivating for engineers, and the same source warns that badly scoped hard problems push people away. Nothing found supports the specific apparatus: sealing a queue, the month-ten eligibility gate, or one-at-a-time release. Broader retention literature in the same search ranks advancement, pay and recognition above challenge as retention drivers, so treat scarcity-of-hard-problems as a motivator, not a retention lever on its own.*

It ranks here because first refusal on a genuinely hard problem is one of the few things a larger employer structurally cannot offer a specific person, and withholding your hardest unstarted work from month-one hires costs nothing to try and is reversible in a week.

- **What has to be true:** You actually have two or three problems hard enough to be worth waiting for, and the business can tolerate them staying unstarted for the better part of a year.
- **Failure mode / cost:** If the queue is theatre — work that is unpleasant rather than hard — it is transparent on first contact and costs you the credibility you were spending it to build; and someone who leaves mid-problem now leaves a larger hole than before.
- **Who runs it:** Whoever sets the technical roadmap, and they need enough standing to keep a valuable problem deliberately unassigned while people ask why.

- Disclose the proprietary internals in staged degrees at fixed tenure thresholds, with each stage genuinely unavailable earlier and useless out of context, as Masonic degrees release knowledge on a fixed progression.
- No humans: let a system escalate each person's production permissions and blast radius purely as a function of tenure months, with the month-eighteen step the largest and irreversible.
- *Proposed by 3 of the 9 passes.*

### 3. Grant personal hiring authority over a team they recruit

Let anyone past 18 months propose a new unit, and if accepted give them the headcount requisitions, budget line and hiring authority to staff it themselves.

*Checked — [insperity.com](https://www.insperity.com/blog/what-is-intrapreneurship-and-why-should-it-be-part-of-your-hr-strategy/)*

*Note — Confirms that intrapreneurship programs — employees proposing and running internal ventures with dedicated budget and manpower — are a real, documented practice with a claimed retention effect. The sources are practitioner/advisory writing, not controlled evidence, and none of them describe handing the proposer headcount requisitions and independent hiring authority, or an 18-month eligibility threshold. The delegation depth this option assumes is beyond what any source shows.*

It ranks here because founding and staffing a team is the thing a mid-career engineer leaves to go and do, and it is far easier to grant inside a company your size than inside the one recruiting them — the eligibility gate then makes tenure the price of admission.

- **What has to be true:** You are growing enough to have headcount worth handing over, and you can live with a hiring bar set by someone who has never hired before.
- **Failure mode / cost:** A bad hire made under personal authority is politically expensive to reverse, and a rejected proposal is an accelerant — someone who pitches a unit and is turned down leaves faster than if you had never opened the door.
- **Who runs it:** The founder or CTO; this is a delegation of a hiring mandate and nobody below that level can actually grant it.

- Give the specialist unilateral authority to hire three people onto a budget they control for five years, with the authority written as a personal grant that dies with their employment.
- Let each specialist personally hire and direct two people of their choosing on a problem they chose, so leaving means abandoning colleagues they recruited rather than colleagues assigned to them.
- Let the specialist become the employer of a two-person team they hire, budget and pay from a P&L you assign them, so leaving means dissolving people who work for them personally.
- *Proposed by 4 of the 9 passes.*

## The next 10

### 4. Personal spend authority scaling with tenure

Give each person past twelve months a discretionary capital budget they spend unilaterally with no approval, scaling with tenure, reported after the fact.

*Checked — [qz.com](https://qz.com/954675/this-company-trusts-its-employees-so-much-it-has-a-no-limits-expense-policy)*

*Note — Confirms a large firm runs unilateral, no-prior-approval employee spending with after-the-fact review, and reports it saved money. It does not support the two distinguishing features of this option: a per-person discretionary capital budget that scales with tenure, and any twelve-month eligibility gate. Netflix's version is uncapped judgment on business expenses for everyone, not a tenure-graded capital allowance; a parallel search found most firms pair employee discretion with card-level limits and an approval threshold above a set dollar amount.*

- Give the specialist personal budget authority — a real number they sign against without approval — and raise it each quarter based on realised outcomes, making spending power the thing they'd surrender.
- Hand over legal signing authority and a bank mandate on day one, so the scarce good on offer is elapsed time rather than scope.
- Make the specialist the purchaser of internal services: give them an annual budget in real currency to buy compute, contractors, designers and legal from inside the firm, forfeited entirely on departure.
- *Proposed by 4 of the 9 passes.*

### 5. Stamp a named owner into each live system and byline

Spending almost nothing: stamp a named maintainer into every internal system's docs and code headers — 'the X service, maintained by <person>' — transferable only by that person's own signed handoff.

*Checked — [github.blog](https://github.blog/engineering/architecture-optimization/how-we-organize-and-get-things-done-with-serviceowners/)*

*Note — Confirms the cheap mechanism: machine-readable named ownership stamped next to the code (CODEOWNERS/SERVICEOWNERS) is standard practice and is credited with preventing code rot because everyone knows who to go to. Two gaps: at GitHub and in the CODEOWNERS convention generally, ownership is assigned to teams rather than named individuals, and ownership entries are routinely reassigned or garbage-collected by automation (tools like cleanowners remove orphaned entries) — the opposite of transfer only by the owner's own signed handoff. The naming is confirmed; the individual, non-revocable form is not.*

- Write the person's name into the shipped artifact as its published author, and keep publishing under that name only while they remain.
- For one named person: rename the internal platform, protocol or file format after them, in production and in public documentation, before month twelve.
- Post permanent physical boards in the building recording every completed system, its date, and every name on it, unveiled at a ceremony, the way change-ringing towers hang peal boards.
- Permanently attach the person's name to the systems they originate in a public registry the firm maintains and keeps updating for decades, the way first-ascent registries credit climbing routes.
- *Merged in, and previously headed:* Permanent public registry of who built what
- *Proposed by 3 of the 9 passes.*

### 6. Pay a bounty for forwarding every inbound recruiter offer

Contractually route inbound recruiter offers through the firm, pay a bounty for each forwarded, and commit to matching or beating by published formula within seventy-two hours.

*Not verified*

*Note — A follow-up search ('employment contract requiring employee to disclose outside job offers to employer enforceability') also settled nothing. General counteroffer sources exist, but nothing found describes a contractual duty to route inbound recruiter approaches through the employer, a per-offer bounty, or a published matching formula on a 72-hour clock, and nothing found addresses whether such a duty is enforceable.*

- Turn the outside offer into an asset you buy: pay the specialist a standing quarterly fee to forward every unsolicited approach, price and terms, and use the aggregated data as a product you sell back to peers.
- Pay a public bounty for forwarding every unsolicited approach to a shared board, the way Pseudomyrmex acacia-ants patrol the host and attack encroaching vines and browsers on sight.
- Pay a quarterly bonus for forwarding unsolicited recruiter mail into a shared channel where the firm posts, publicly, what it would and would not match.
- *Merged in, and previously headed:* Bounty for forwarding recruiter approaches to a public board
- *Proposed by 4 of the 9 passes.*

### 7. Engineer the ramp down to weeks so the 12-month clock stops ruling

Pay the first eight weeks entirely for writing the ramp path and tooling for their own role, so full effectiveness arrives at month three and the twelve-month clock never sets the rhythm.

*Checked — [trainual.com](https://trainual.com/manual/how-to-measure-time-to-productivity)*

*Note — Confirms that a three-month ramp to full effectiveness is at the fast end of a normal range, so the timeline the option assumes is realistic rather than fanciful. It does not support the specific device: nothing found shows employers paying the first eight weeks purely for the hire to author the ramp path and tooling for their own role, and nothing addresses the claimed retention effect on a twelve-month clock.*

- Compress ramp to 90 days with a paid full-time overlap shadow and a pre-built environment, so the hardest work starts in month four rather than month thirteen.
- Treat the twelve-month ramp as a variable rather than a constant: fund a standing team whose only measured output is cutting time-to-first-independent-shipment to six weeks.
- *Proposed by 3 of the 9 passes.*

### 8. Back-load pay into accruals forfeited on early exit

Back-load the wage curve: 70 percent of market for months zero to twelve, 140 percent from month eighteen, with the accrued gap stated as a running number.

*Checked — [sec.gov](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001069353/000089383899000345/0000893838-99-000345.txt)*

*Note — Confirms the mechanism: deliberately depressing current base pay and paying it later is a real, documented retention structure. It does not support the option's parameters — no source found for a 70 percent / 140 percent split, an eighteen-month crossover, or the claim that publishing a running accrued-gap number changes departure behavior.*

- Replace open-ended employment with a two-year fixed term carrying a completion payment of six months' salary, forfeited entirely on early exit.
- No humans: accrue deferred cash by the hour, paid only on anniversaries, with the accrual rate doubling after month eighteen and no person authorised to grant exceptions.
- Hire on voyage articles: fixed multi-year terms tied to a named mission, with the accumulated wage paid as a lump at term's end, as merchant seamen sign ship's articles per voyage.
- *Proposed by 3 of the 9 passes.*

### 9. Own the named client account and its fee stream

Make the person co-owner of the customer relationship with a contractual revenue share on named accounts that survives only under this firm's paper.

*Checked — [troutman.com](https://www.troutman.com/insights/easy-come-easy-go-state-rules-on-post-termination-forfeitures-of-bonuses-and-commissions/)*

*Note — Confirms that a revenue share which lapses on departure — 'survives only under this firm's paper' — is enforceable in some states with clear drafting. It does not hold everywhere: the same sources state that in California and New York earned commissions are treated as wages and cannot be forfeited by contract, so the option's central lock fails outright in two of the largest employment markets.*

- Give the specialist a named customer account they own commercially — they sign the contract, they get a percentage of its revenue for as long as the account renews and they remain the signatory.
- Convert people at 18 months onto a partner-style arrangement: a percentage of fees on work they originate, paid for as long as the client stays.
- Grant exclusive territory over a product line with a revenue share, a right of first refusal to buy it, and enforced standards, the way franchise agreements assign protected territories.
- *Merged in, and previously headed:* Franchise-style exclusive territory over a product line
- *Proposed by 4 of the 9 passes.*

### 10. Guaranteed unconditional right to return to the same seat

Offer a guaranteed seat back within twelve months, in writing, to anyone who takes a job at a larger employer, with tenure and deferred payouts continuing.

*Checked — [lattice.com](https://lattice.com/templates/former-employee-rehire-boomerang-policy-template)*

*Note — Confirms that formal written boomerang-rehire policies exist and that twelve months is a real dividing line for bridging tenure and benefits, which is the part of the option that has to be true for it to work. It does not support the 'guaranteed seat': the sources describe priority consideration or guaranteed review of an alumni application, not a guaranteed offer, and nothing found addresses deferred payouts continuing during the absence.*

- Grant a standing right to take an outside job for up to two years and return to the same seat with tenure, stake and vesting clock unbroken, exercisable once.
- By Friday: hand every specialist an undated, unconditional re-entry contract letting them return within five years at their departure level with no interview and no approval.
- Require a mandatory two-year unpaid recall option in every contract, with a retainer paid throughout, so departure is structurally a leave rather than a break, as ballet companies retain guest-artist first call.
- Write the specialist a transferable ten-year call option on their own job at today's title and terms, exercisable at any time, so departure is a suspension rather than an end.
- *Proposed by 5 of the 9 passes.*

### 11. Gate new work on handing off or automating the old

Require every specialist to automate their previous job before starting the next one, and pay a bonus scaled to how much of their old role the machine now performs.

*Proposal — nothing to verify*

*Note — This is a proposal about internal policy design (automate your prior role before rotating; bonus scaled to the share of the old role now machine-performed). It asserts no fact about the outside world that a source could confirm or contradict, so no search was run. Whether such a scheme produces the claimed behaviour would be an empirical question only after it exists.*

- Allocate the highest-value projects only to people who have already deposited a named successor into that same project, the way yuccas abort fruit from moths that oviposit without pollinating.

### 12. Hire only people already ramped at their own expense

Recruit only from people already ramped at their own expense — your customers, your contractors, and outside developers who have shipped against your API.

*Checked — [nextmantra.ai](https://nextmantra.ai/blog/developer-communities-recruiting)*

*Note — The source supports the weaker claim that hiring from developer communities already engaged with your stack yields better fit and retention. It does not support the option's exclusivity ("recruit only from"), does not cover customers or contractors as sources, and gives no evidence on ramp-time savings or on whether such a pool is large enough to staff from alone. The source is a recruiting-vendor blog, not a controlled study.*

### 13. Staff support that strips overhead off senior people

Fund a standing two-person unit whose only job is stripping admin, procurement and recruiter noise off senior people, like Pseudonocardia bacteria on leafcutter ant cuticles secreting antibiotics against Escovopsis.

*Checked — [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-018-04520-1)*

*Note — The load-bearing biology checks out on all three points: Pseudonocardia actinobacteria are carried on the ant cuticle, they secrete antifungal metabolites, and those suppress the specialised garden parasite Escovopsis (originally Currie et al., Nature 1999, https://www.nature.com/articles/19519). One qualification the analogy should absorb: the same 2018 paper shows Escovopsis counter-attacks with metabolites (melinacidin IV, shearinine D) that inhibit Pseudonocardia itself, so the defence is a contested arms race rather than a stable shield. Some protective strains are Streptomyces rather than Pseudonocardia.*

- Install a signal any member can pull that forcibly reallocates support staff within a week, the way a honeybee's tremble dance recruits more receivers when nectar processing is the bottleneck.

## The rest, in rank order

*Not checked by search. Verification covers the lead option of each of the top 13 families only, so the outside-world claims below are unverified — ask me to check any of them and I will.* — families 14 through 114 continue in [the file](computer:///sessions/local_dy2girmvi5/mnt/outputs/20260901-052952/report.md), each with its variants, ending with the closing read.

---

What I would look at first, and what would change it: start with #1 on the three people you would least like to lose, and pair it with #5, which costs almost nothing and is reversible — but before any of it, spend an hour testing the premise you ruled out, because "we benchmark and we match" is almost always benchmarked against day-one offers, while the comparison an engineer actually runs at month 18 is whatever is left unvested and unrealised on their side against a large employer's liquid annual refresher plus a fresh grant; compute realizable 24-month value for the last three people who left versus the offer they took, and if the gap is over about 10% then it is still the money and most of this list is the wrong list. Two things you know and I do not: whether the leavers all came from one or two teams, which would make this a manager problem wearing a tenure disguise, and whether they went to bigger companies for the work or for the liquidity, which decides whether the top of this list or #8 and #10 is your lever.

One WARN from the integrity check: 15 pairs sit inside a family after being adjudicated apart. I read the three families named — margin share, routing work through an unmatched asset, and the internal time auction — and each names one mechanism, so I left them whole. Sub-agent file tools needed absolute paths, so all nine generators were re-dispatched with them; nothing else was degraded.

1	---
2	name: creative-problem-solving
3	description: Runs a long pipeline that generates hundreds of options for an open-ended problem across many isolated angles, checks the ones it presents most prominently by search, and presents every option it generated rather than a pruned few. Use ONLY when the user explicitly asks for it: the /ideas command, naming this skill, or saying "use creative problem solving on this". Do NOT select it merely because a prompt asks for ideas, options, angles, approaches, a brainstorm or a rethink, or says the obvious answers are spent — those are ordinary requests and answering them directly is almost always right. The cost is the reason: a full run takes about forty minutes and returns a long document, so it must be the user's deliberate choice and not an inference from phrasing. Not for problems with one correct answer, or for executing an idea already chosen.
4	compatibility: Requires sub-agent dispatch, python3 and a Bash tool to run the full pipeline; without them it degrades to sequential passes in a single context and says so. Uses web search to verify options.
5	metadata:
6	  author: Yaniv Golan
7	  email: yaniv@golan.name
8	  version: 0.3.0
9	---
10	
11	# Creative problem solving
12	
13	Named creativity frameworks mostly don't work on their own — in head-to-head testing,
14	SCAMPER and similar scored no better than a plain prompt, and some scored worse. What has
15	evidence behind it is narrower — reaching past the answer you would give first, rather than
16	decorating a single sweep with headings. This pipeline does that by generating each pass blind
17	under its own constraint, and by asking for enough options that the obvious ones are spent
18	early.
19	
20	So this is an engine, not a menu: the classic methods survive only as **constraint lenses**
21	applied one at a time. *Structure that makes the next idea harder to reach for helps; structure
22	that decorates a single sweep produces longer output that scores better and isn't better.*
23	
24	## When not to use this
25	
26	Problems with one correct answer, debugging, executing an already-chosen idea, or anything where
27	the user wants a decision rather than options. A four-phase divergence engine on "which of these
28	two should I pick" is the same mistake in the opposite direction.
29	
30	## Reference files
31	
32	- `references/pipeline.md` — the operative stages: sub-agent per stage, the file each writes,
33	  the scripts that check them. **Required reading before Phase 1**, not optional depth.
34	- `references/report.md` — the whole of Phase 4. **Required before you write anything the user
35	  sees.**
36	- `references/pruning.md` — the Phase 3 steps. **Required before you prune.**
37	- `references/gotchas.md` — the failure modes this pipeline actually produces (framework theater,
38	  temperature, premature convergence and the rest), with what each one costs. Read it when
39	  something is going wrong, or once before your first run.
40	- `references/lenses.md` — longer worked prompts per lens, plus the demoted ones (SCAMPER, Six
41	  Thinking Hats) and why. **Optional**: the Phase 1 table carries both moves for every lens. Read
42	  it when a lens isn't landing, not as routine.
43	- `references/evidence.md` — what the research supports, and how strongly. Read if the user
44	  challenges the approach, or before skipping or changing a phase.
45	
46	**If this file appears to end early, it did — re-read it from disk before continuing.** A long

1	# The pipeline
2	
3	The operational detail behind Phases 1-4: which sub-agent runs each stage, what each writes, and
4	which script checks it. **Read this before generating anything** — you cannot run the steps
5	without it, and every stage after generation depends on the file the stage before it wrote.
6	
7	This is the same pipeline whichever way the skill was invoked. The `/ideas` command exists only
8	to make invocation reliable; it does not change what runs.
9	
10	Several rules below carry a short piece of evidence — a run that did the other thing. The full
11	narratives live in `docs/INCIDENTS.md` **in the repository**, which does not ship with the skill and
12	which you do not need: every rule here is complete as written. Read it when deciding whether a rule
13	can be relaxed, not when following one.
14	
15	Requires sub-agent dispatch, `python3` and a Bash tool. Those three fail differently and the
16	fallbacks are not interchangeable.
17	
18	**No sub-agent dispatch** — run the lenses as sequential passes in your own context, per
19	`SKILL.md` Phase 1. That fallback is written there and you must disclose taking it.
20	
21	**No Bash or no `python3`** — the scripts do not ship in the zip or the `.agents/` mirror either,
22	so this is the normal case on those install routes rather than an exotic one. The pipeline still
23	runs: every stage below is a thing a model does, and only the checks between them are executable.
24	What you lose is worth naming to the reader in one line, because these are the guarantees this
25	skill advertises:
26	
27	- **The integrity check** (`verify_pipeline.py`). Nothing proves `generated == presented +
28	  rejected`. Do the arithmetic yourself and state the three numbers; a count you did by hand is
29	  weaker evidence than a count a script refused to skip, and the reader should know which they got.
30	- **The generated report skeleton** (`build_report.py`). You assemble the report by hand, so the
31	  guarantee that every option reaches the page becomes an intention rather than a construction —
32	  and the depth fields for the leading options stop being enforced slots and become a template you
33	  have to remember. Work from the family list in rank order and do not summarise it.
34	- **The adjudicator agreement probe** (`shard_candidates.py`, `merge_relations.py`). No pairs are
35	  double-judged, so the run measures nothing about how stable its own grouping is. Say so rather
36	  than reporting a grouping as though its reliability were known.
37	
38	Sharding and merging themselves you can do in your own context; they cost context rather than
39	correctness. **Say in one line which of these you lost.** A run that quietly drops the checks and
40	describes itself in the same words as a checked run is the failure this whole pipeline exists to
41	prevent.
42	
43	## When a script refuses: retry once, correcting it, then stop
44	
45	Every check below names the stage that wrote the file it refused, and several say to re-dispatch
46	only that stage. Two rules bound that.
47	
48	**Carry the correction into the retry.** A bare re-run with the prompt that produced the file is
49	the least likely thing to work: these files are refused for what was asked for, not for luck. Add
50	the one line the failure names — for a refused pool, *"write only the JSON value, with no prose and
51	no code fence"*; for a shard that claimed an option from a cluster it did not own, the cluster it
52	owns.
53	
54	**A second identical failure ends it.** Do not dispatch a third time. Say which stage refused,
55	repeat the failure line verbatim, and give the reader what the run has while naming what is missing
56	from it. On a recorded run a structural gate failed and then failed again byte-for-byte identically,
57	seconds apart; the same failure twice is a fact about the prompt, and a third attempt spends minutes
58	to learn it again.
59	
60	Two costs are worth knowing before spending a retry. A refused pool is caught at step 4, by
61	`shard_candidates.py`, before any later stage exists — so re-dispatching one generator there is
62	cheap and loses nothing. Re-running `merge_families.py` after ranking is not: it invalidates steps 7
63	and 8, which must both be re-run, in that order.
64	
65	## Step 0 — resolve `$CPS` before any other step
66	
67	Every script below is called as `python3 "$CPS/scripts/<name>.py"`. Resolve `CPS` once, first,
68	with the block below. Run it exactly as written and read the `CPS=` line it prints.
69	
70	**Why it is a search and not an edit.** The path you read this file at is a **file-tool** path.
71	The scripts are run by the **shell**. On some hosts those are different filesystem namespaces —
72	not different working directories, different mounts of the same content at different absolute
73	paths — and there is **no string that is correct for both**. On Cowork's host loop the file tools
74	report the plugin under the user's home directory while the shell sees it under
75	`/sessions/<session>/mnt/.remote-plugins/<plugin id>`. Stripping a known tail off the first
76	produces a path the shell cannot stat, and an upward walk from it searches a tree that is not
77	there — so both halves of the old instruction failed together, for one shared reason, and
78	produced "scripts not found" on a host where the scripts were present and working.
79	
80	That is a different problem from Step 0b's, and it has a different answer. Step 0b's run directory
81	is one place with **two spellings**, so each tool family is handed the spelling it accepts. The
82	plugin root is **two places**, so the shell has to find its own.
83	
84	```sh
85	# CPS-RESOLVER — executable as written; the test suite extracts and runs this block.
86	cps_resolve() {                    # $1 = the path you read THIS file at
87	  READ_AT="$1"
88	  SENTINEL="scripts/verify_pipeline.py"
89	  # The COMPLETE root list, overridable as one variable, ONE ROOT PER LINE. Not a default plus a hard-coded
90	  # tail: a search with roots the caller cannot control cannot be tested, because the fixture
91	  # cannot stop it reaching the real install and answering correctly for the wrong reason.
92	  #
93	  # ONE ROOT PER LINE, not space-separated. Desktop's local agent mode stages plugins under
94	  # "$HOME/Library/Application Support/Claude/local-agent-mode-sessions/<session>/<sub>/rpm/", and
95	  # a space-separated list word-splits "Application Support" into two roots that do not exist.
96	  # Measured on a machine with that shape: the old three roots returned ZERO hits while a
97	  # complete install sat under Application Support -- branch 1 happened to save it, and would not
98	  # have on a split host.
99	  ROOTS="${CPS_SEARCH_ROOTS:-$(printf '%s\n' /sessions "$HOME/.claude/plugins" "$HOME/.claude" "$HOME/Library/Application Support/Claude")}"
100	  CAND="${READ_AT%/skills/creative-problem-solving/references/pipeline.md}"
101	  PID=$(basename "$CAND")
102	
103	  # Branch 1 — the string edit, VERIFIED rather than trusted. Free, and guaranteed to be the
104	  # same install as the file you just read, which no other branch can promise.
105	  if [ -f "$CAND/$SENTINEL" ]; then
106	    CPS="$CAND"; echo "CPS=$CPS (branch 1: path as read)"; return 0
107	  fi
108	
109	  # Between the branches: if the shell CAN see the directory the file tools named, it can judge
110	  # this install directly, and searching elsewhere would be a mistake rather than a fallback.
111	  # A skills-only install (the zip, the .agents mirror, an older version that shipped skills/ and
112	  # nothing else) reaches this point legitimately, and the global search below would bind it to a
113	  # DIFFERENT version's scripts sitting elsewhere on the same disk — or refuse because two of them
114	  # are. Measured locally: reading pipeline.md from a cached 0.1.0 (skills/ only) refused with two
115	  # copies found, instead of taking the documented scriptless fallback written for exactly it.
116	  #
117	  # Gated on visibility, and that gate is load-bearing. On a split-namespace host $CAND is a path
118	  # from the OTHER filesystem: `[ -d "$CAND" ]` is false there not because the install is odd but
119	  # because the shell cannot see it. Measured on Cowork host loop — the file tools report the
120	  # plugin somewhere under the user's own home directory (deliberately not spelled out here: a
121	  # literal host path in this file becomes model-visible text and trips the runtime host-path
122	  # guard, which is how this very line was caught) while the shell has the same plugin under
123	  # /sessions/<id>/mnt/.remote-plugins/. If
124	  # this test ran unconditionally, every host-loop run would conclude "scriptless" and take the
125	  # degraded path, which is the exact silent downgrade this whole block exists to prevent.
126	  if [ -d "$CAND" ]; then
127	    if [ -d "$CAND/agents" ] || [ -d "$CAND/../agents" ]; then
128	      echo "REFUSING: $CAND is a plugin install — it has an agents/ directory — but carries no"
129	      echo "  $SENTINEL. Its scripts are missing. Another copy elsewhere on this disk is a"
130	      echo "  DIFFERENT version, and running its scripts against these instructions is the"
131	      echo "  version skew this step exists to prevent. Reinstall the plugin, or set CPS by hand."
132	      return 2
133	    fi
134	    echo "CPS= (branch 1b: visible install with no scripts/ and no agents/ — this is the zip, the"
135	    echo "  .agents/ mirror, or a skills-only version. They ship without scripts/ by design. Take"
136	    echo "  the SKILL.md Phase 1 fallback and say in one line which checks the run lost.)"
137	    return 1
138	  fi
139	
140	  # $CAND is not visible. That has TWO causes wanting different answers, and `[ -d ]` alone
141	  # cannot tell them apart: the path belongs to another filesystem, or it is simply wrong.
142	  # Decide it without ever stat-ing a path from the other side — the shell's own location and the
143	  # read path's shape are enough. Under Cowork's host loop the shell sits under /sessions/ and the
144	  # file tools report a host path that does not; under its VM loop BOTH are under /sessions/, so
145	  # a missing directory there really is missing.
146	  SPLIT=0
147

5	**Required before you prune anything.** It is a reference rather than skill body because the skill
6	body is truncated at a fixed length in a long conversation, and everything from here on sat past
7	that cut. Read on demand it arrives whole.
8	
9	**If you are pruning and cannot recall the order of the steps or what counts as a legitimate edit,
10	read this file again.** A reference compacted out of a long conversation leaves no marker saying it
11	is gone.
12	
13	---
14	
15	**Critique for feasibility. Never critique for novelty.** Self-refinement pulls ideas back
16	toward the domain prototype, and sycophancy grows across a session, so late-loop critique
17	is the most flattering and least useful. Once an idea exists its novelty is fixed; the
18	only legitimate edits are killing it, merging duplicates, or noting what it costs.
19	
20	Run these in order, once. No second refinement loop.
21	
22	1. **Find the convergences by reading.** Read the pool and ask: which
23	   *mechanism* shows up more than once, however differently worded? Repetition is
24	   information — a move four of five passes arrive at is likely the attractor of the
25	   problem space, and belongs in the answer rather than being silently deduped. It is
26	   evidence of an attractor only to the extent the passes started apart: identical briefs
27	   produce agreement that means nothing, so say *how many passes proposed it* and make no
28	   claim about how they got there.
29	
30	   By reading — there is no tool for this. No surface-level scorer can see that two
31	   differently-worded ideas share a mechanism; one was built for this pipeline, run
32	   across six iterations, and false-negatived on exactly that signal every time. This
33	   judgement is the grouping stage's, and `references/pipeline.md` says which sub-agent makes
34	   it.
35	
36	   **Lead with the claim about the problem, not with the count.** "Every route into this ends
37	   up renting permissions" is the finding; the count is the evidence under it, not the headline.
38	   `build_report.py` prints the count itself, as `Proposed by N of the 9 passes`, wherever a
39	   family drew members from three or more pools — so you do not write that line yourself, and you
40	   do not dress it up as separate discovery. Every pass worked from the same sharpened brief, and
41	   on the first live run seven of nine generator briefs were byte-identical. What convergence
42	   tells the reader is something about the problem, and that is all it tells them.
43	2. **Assemble, if the user asked for a thing rather than a list.** The passes produce
44	   tactics; "a new model for X" wants a coherent whole. Group compatible mechanisms into
45	   internally consistent wholes and name each. This is composing, not the polishing
46	   banned above. The line: combining ideas into a coherent model is allowed; making an
47	   idea sound better, safer, or more marketable is not. If you catch yourself softening an
48	   idea so it sounds sensible, stop — that's the regression.
49	3. **Cross-consistency prune.** For every idea, ask what it requires to be true. Kill the
50	   ones whose requirements contradict *each other* — an idea that cannot hold together
51	   internally is not an option. An idea that collides with a constraint the user stated is a
52	   different case: it ships, with the collision named in its failure-mode line. You are not the
53	   veto. The reader's veto is better informed than yours and costs them seconds; a suppressed
54	   option costs them the whole idea.
55	4. **Handle borrowed mechanisms.** Any idea resting on a claim about the outside world —
56	   how an organism works, how another industry solved something, what a company actually
57	   did — is a hallucination risk. This covers *all* analogies, not just biological ones; a
58	   misremembered historical example reads just as fluent as an invented organism.
59	   - **Verify by search the ones you will present prominently** — the top 3 and the next 10.
60	     If a mechanism does not verify, cut it; a borrowed mechanism that isn't real is not an
61	     option, it is a fabrication that reads as confident.
62	   - **Everything below the top 13 ships unverified and is labelled so**, with a standing offer
63	     to verify any of them on request. Do not quietly present unchecked outside claims at the
64	     same confidence as checked ones. `build_report.py` writes that label and that offer; you do
65	     not add them.
66	   - **With no search available, cut nothing.** "Does not verify" means a search ran and failed,
67	     which cannot happen where no search can run — so the rule above does not apply and the
68	     prominent options keep their borrowed mechanisms. State each as a principle rather than a
69	     citation ("systems that meter a scarce resource tend to…", not "Company X did this"), drop
70	     the specific attribution you cannot check rather than the idea resting on it, and say once
71	     at the top that no search was available. A named downgrade is honest; a silent one is the
72	     one failure this pipeline cannot survive.
73	
74	---

1	# Phase 4 — writing the report
2	
3	The whole of Phase 4: what the reader gets, the shape of an option, what happens when the answer
4	becomes a document, and the honesty rule. `SKILL.md` carries the one-paragraph version and sends
5	you here.
6	
7	**This is required reading before you write anything the user sees.** It is a reference rather than
8	part of the skill body for one reason: the skill body is truncated at a fixed length in a long
9	conversation, and Phase 4 sat past that cut — so the phase that produces the answer was the part
10	most likely to be missing when it was needed. Here it is read on demand and arrives whole.
11	
12	**One consequence to know.** A reference read into a long conversation can be compacted away like
13	any other content, and unlike a truncated skill body it leaves no marker saying so. If you are
14	writing the report and cannot recall the option shape or the honesty rule, read this file again
15	rather than reconstructing them.
16	
17	---
18	
19	The reader ends with a file they can open and keep, not only a long message. On the scripted path
20	`build_report.py` writes it and step 10 presents it; on the no-script fallback you write it
21	yourself. This is not conditional on the user asking.
22	
23	**Phases 0-3 are working state, not deliverable.** The user gets the ideas and the
24	judgement — not the brief you sharpened, not the lens names, not the cluster analysis.
25	Showing your process is the single easiest way to triple the word
26	count without adding information. In testing, skill responses ran 2-3× the length of a
27	plain answer and roughly half of that was apparatus.
28	
29	**If the cause of the problem isn't known, diagnosis comes first.** When the user reports a
30	symptom — a number that moved, something that stopped working — open with the candidate
31	causes and the cheapest way to tell them apart, *then* the options. If the reader has to
32	know which cause is live before any of your ideas apply, they need that first. Keep it to
33	about three lines: this is a signpost, not a section, and on a light question it will eat a
34	third of your budget if you let it.
35	
36	The most-repeated failure here, and it never feels like padding — each clause earns its
37	place and the paragraph still lands at triple budget. The tell: a diagnosis that lists its
38	candidate causes *and* argues for each. Name them, give the test, stop. (Observed: 157 words.)
39	
40	```
41	[If a reading was chosen for an ambiguous problem: one line naming it.]
42	[If cause is unknown: 2-4 candidate causes + the cheapest test to tell them apart. ~3 lines.]
43	[HARD CEILING on those two together: 4 lines, ~100 words. They often overlap — the reading
44	 you picked is frequently one of the candidate causes — and you may merge them into one
45	 short paragraph, but merging buys no extra length. Then stop and start the first option.]
46	
47	### [Idea name]
48	[2-3 sentences: the mechanism first, then what it produces.]
49	- What has to be true: [the load-bearing assumption]
50	- Failure mode / cost: [one line]
51	- Who runs it: [required whenever it needs people or a mandate the asker doesn't have]
52	
53	[…several of these, in the rank order the pipeline produced — see `references/pipeline.md`
54	step 7, which ranks by whether an option would survive vetting…]
55	
56	**Checked and failed:** [only options a search refuted, each with its source]
57	**What I'd look at first, and what would change that:** [your actual read + 1-2 things
58	the user knows and you don't]
59	```
60	
61	**Every option you generated appears in the answer.** Options proposing the same core
62	intervention are grouped into a family and shown together, the strongest leading and the rest
63	as one-line variants naming what differs. A mechanism four passes reached gets one place, not
64	four — but all four stay visible. Nothing is dropped for being similar to something else: a
65	wrong merge is unrecoverable, since the reader never learns the option existed, while a wrong
66	grouping costs them a line of reading.
67	
68	Only two things leave the list. An option whose own description concedes it does not answer the
69	question asked, and a borrowed mechanism that a search refuted — and the second is reported as
70	checked-and-failed, with the source, rather than deleted quietly.
71	
72	**Depth is what scales with the question, not count.** A light question gets the same complete
73	list with two bullets per option and one line of closing read; a strategic one gets three
74	bullets, a ranking and a fuller read. Keep each option to about four lines of prose: word
75	counts are a poor target because you cannot reliably count your own words, so a word budget
76	produces confident non-compliance.
77	
78	**Always end with a point of view.** On a light question that's one line, not a section — an
79	answer that lists options and declines to say which you'd pick has handed the work back.
80	
81	The raised ceilings are a **reallocation, not an expansion**. The budget comes from the cut
82	list, which shrinks as fewer ideas are cut. Options past the first four or five carry their
83	mechanism and a one-line risk and nothing else — a compact entry the reader can evaluate in a
84	few seconds. An option worth one line is worth more than an option that isn't there; an option
85	padded to four lines to look like the others is the failure above, wearing a new hat.
86	
87	**Present only live options.** This is narrower than it sounds, and it does not conflict with
88	Phase 3 step 3. That step says an option needing people the asker doesn't have is still worth
89	presenting *with that named* — "you'd need to hire someone who has run this" is useful.
90	What leaves the list is an option whose own description concedes it isn't the thing the user
91	asked for: "that's a different firm", "you'd now be an insurance business". The test is not
92	"is this hard to staff" but "does this still answer the question asked." Say so in a line
93	rather than deleting it silently.
94	
95	**And the inverse, which matters more.** Everything mechanically distinct that *does* answer the
96	question ships as an option. Duplicates are grouped, not dropped, and nothing leaves for being
97	an idea you suspect the reader will reject. Readers who asked for options are doing the rejecting; that is
98	what the failure-mode line is for. A promising option you buried is invisible to them, and
99	invisible is the one outcome they cannot recover from. When you are unsure whether something
100	survives, present it in compact form rather than cutting it.
101	
102	**Ordering and judgement are different jobs, and they will disagree.** The order is the
103	pipeline's: families arrive ranked by whether they would survive vetting (`references/pipeline.md`
104	step 7). What stops the safe idea burying the interesting ones is not the order but the rule that
105	nothing is cut — a strange option is never ranked out of existence, only ranked. Then say what
106	you'd actually look at first in the closing read, often not the top-ranked one. That divergence is
107	information, not an inconsistency: say both. And don't promise a ranking you don't give.
108	
109	Lead with the mechanism, not the benefit — a benefit-first idea is indistinguishable from
110	a slogan.
111	
112	The template is a **floor, not a form**. If an idea has nothing to say under a line, drop
113	the line. Three things that look like content and aren't:
114	
115	- *"Why it's not the obvious answer"* under every idea — you're arguing with a baseline the
116	  reader can't see. State the obvious answer once at the top if it's genuinely useful, or
117	  not at all.
118	- *The sharpened brief* as a section — it reads as jargon restatement of what they just
119	  told you.
120	### When the answer becomes a document
121	
122	Often the run ends in a file — a memo, a brief, a deck — asked for after the report. That
123	composition is a fresh generation pass with none of Phase 3's constraints attached, and it is
124	where a pruned pipeline grows back: hedged options harden into committed policy, *what has to be
125	true* and *who runs it* quietly drop out, and specificity the pipeline never produced gets
126	invented to fill a section out.
127	
128	- **Every number, threshold and named policy in the document must trace to pipeline output or
129	  to something the user gave you.** What traces to neither is invented — cut it, or write it as
130	  the open choice it is. A threshold that arrived only because the section needed one reads as
131	  authoritative precisely because nothing in the run ever argued for it.
132	- **Black-hat the document, not the pool.** The contradictions that matter are between sections
133	  written separately that were never adjacent until now — at Phase 3 they did not exist yet.
134	
135	### The honesty rule
136	
137	Treat **diversity as measurable, novelty as a hypothesis, feasibility as the user's
138	decision.** (Diversity is measured in the repo's eval lane, never in the answer.) This is
139	calibration, not modesty: model novelty judgements diverge from expert
140	judgement even when the reasoning looks sound, experts disagree with each other on
141	feasibility, and pre-execution novelty ratings have been shown to reverse once someone
142	actually builds the thing.
143	
144	So never write "this is a novel idea." Write "I did not find prior art for this — here's
145	where I looked, and here's who would already be doing it if it were obvious." The second
146	is falsifiable; the first isn't.
147	
148	**And never describe process that did not happen.** Don't say you ran passes you didn't run,
149	searched what you didn't search, or checked what you didn't check. This is the same rule as
150	above pointed at yourself, and it is the one failure this pipeline cannot survive: every
151	other claim it makes is auditable against the answer, but a process claim is only auditable
152	against the record, so the reader has no defence. If a mode was unavailable, say which and
153	move on — a named downgrade costs one line and keeps everything else worth believing.
154

1	# Constraint lenses
2	
3	Longer worked prompts for the nine lenses. **`SKILL.md`'s Phase 1 table is the operative
4	version** — it carries each lens's move and second move. Read this file when a lens isn't
5	landing, not as routine.
6	
7	## Contents
8	
9	- [Using a lens well](#using-a-lens-well)
10	- [The lenses](#the-lenses) — contradiction, first principles, inversion, constraint
11	  extremity, time-shift, analogical transfer, biomimicry, morphological, actor reversal
12	- [Demoted lenses](#demoted-lenses) — SCAMPER, Six Thinking Hats
13	- [Choosing lenses](#choosing-lenses-for-a-problem) — also condensed in the SKILL.md table
14	
15	---
16	
17	## Using a lens well
18	
19	The lens is a *constraint on the search*, not a template for the output — never fill in its
20	sections as headings. One lens per pass; two at once gives you the average of both.
21	
22	Every lens below has a **second move**, and it is reliably the one that gets skipped. The
23	Phase 1 table in `SKILL.md` carries both moves for all nine, so this file is for when a lens
24	isn't landing and you want the longer version.
25	
26	If a pass returns everything above p=0.3 it collapsed to the modal answer. Redo that one pass
27	with: *"every candidate was a high-probability answer — return 6 more from below p=0.1."*
28	Once only; twice produces noise dressed as novelty.
29	
30	## The lenses
31	
32	### Contradiction (TRIZ, stripped down)
33	
34	> Find the tradeoff that everyone working on this problem quietly accepts as a law of
35	> nature — "you can have X or Y, not both." State it explicitly. Then refuse it: generate
36	> approaches that get X and Y simultaneously, by changing what the system is made of,
37	> when the parts act, or where the boundary sits. If the tradeoff turns out to be a real
38	> physical or economic law, say so and instead attack whichever side of it is only
39	> conventionally true.
40	
41	Classical TRIZ resolution moves, useful as sub-prompts: segment the system into
42	independent parts; take the troublesome part out entirely; give different regions
43	different properties; introduce asymmetry; merge operations in time or space; make one
44	element do several jobs; nest one system inside another; do the required change in
45	advance; invert the direction of the action.
46	
47	Keep the contradiction-naming step — it forces an explicit statement of what's being
48	assumed, and it's why TRIZ survived the evidence review. Drop the 39×39 matrix ceremony.
49	
50	Best for: technical bottlenecks, structural constraints, "we can't do X because Y."
51	
52	### First principles
53	
54	> Strip the problem to what must be true regardless of how anyone currently solves it.
55	> List the current approach's assumptions one by one and mark each: physical law,
56	> economic law, regulation, or convention. Most will be convention. Discard everything
57	> that is convention and rebuild solutions using only the laws that remain. Do not check
58	> your rebuilt solution against how things are currently done.
59	
60	This is essentially task decomposition, the best-evidenced of all the framework-shaped
61	interventions. If you only have budget for one lens, use this one.
62	
63	Best for: mature industries, "that's just how it's done", suspected local minimum.
64	
65	### Inversion
66	
67	> Solve the opposite problem. If the goal is to increase X, generate the most effective
68	> ways to destroy X — be specific and mechanically plausible, not glib. Then invert each
69	> one into a defence or an opportunity. Separately: assume the goal has already been
70	> achieved and work backwards to what must have happened first.
71	
72	Denying the model the move it just made reliably pushes it into novel regions; inversion
73	is the cheapest version of that.
74	
75	Best for: when everything generated so far sounds the same; risk and defensive strategy.
76	
77	### Constraint extremity
78	
79	> Generate solutions under each of these separately, treating each as absolutely binding:
80	> (a) one hundredth of a normal budget for this kind of work; (b) it must work in one week;
81	> (c) no humans
82	> are involved at any step; (d) it must work for exactly one person; (e) it must work at
83	> ten thousand times the scale. Do not soften the constraint into something reasonable —
84	> if a constraint makes the current approach impossible, that's the point, and the
85	> replacement is the idea.
86	
87	Best for: capital-heavy or process-heavy incumbents, cost-structure problems.
88	
89	### Time-shift
90	
91	> Identify the single resource that a problem of this kind is usually scarce and expensive in,
92	> and that is getting cheaper fast. Assume it is free and unlimited. Generate what becomes
93	> possible, then work back to what is buildable on the current price curve. Separately:
94	> identify what becomes scarce *because* that resource became abundant — the new
95	> bottleneck is usually where the value moves.
96	
97	The second half is the valuable half and it's the one models skip. Push on it.
98	
99	Best for: anything touching fast-moving technology; strategy over a multi-year horizon.
100	
101	### Analogical transfer
102	
103	> Describe the problem as a pure function, with all domain vocabulary removed — e.g. "get
104	> a scarce resource to whoever values it most, without a central authority deciding."
105	> Find three fields that solved that same abstract function and are as far as possible
106	> from this domain — not adjacent industries. For each, describe the *mechanism* they
107	> used, then port the mechanism, not the surface features.
108	
109	Analogy mining is the best-evidenced *content* intervention available, and the strength is
110	entirely in the distance — adjacent domains produce adjacent ideas, and the measured
111	benefit grows with semantic distance. Push hard on it; treat a comfortable analogy as a
112	failed one.
113	
114	Best for: when you want structurally novel answers rather than better versions.
115	
116	### Biomimicry
117	
118	> State the function biologically: "how does nature move a fluid without a pump?", "how
119	> does nature defend without armour?" Identify organisms or ecosystems that solve it.
120	> For each you must give BOTH the organism AND the mechanism — the actual physical or
121	> chemical process, at a level someone could look up and check. Then abstract the
122	> principle away from the biology and apply it.
123	
124	Domains worth sweeping: structural (spider silk, bone remodelling, coral, nacre);
125	chemical (photosynthesis, enzyme catalysis, bioluminescence); behavioural (swarm
126	intelligence, symbiosis, quorum sensing, migration); ecological (nutrient cycling,
127	succession, redundancy, decomposition).
128	
129	**Grounding is mandatory.** An organism name with a hand-waved mechanism is the standard
130	failure mode of AI biomimicry — confident and wrong. Search verifies the borrowed mechanism behind
131	the lead option of each of the top 13 families; if it doesn't verify, cut it. A biomimicry option that
132	is a nested variant, or that falls below the top 13, ships unverified — and that label matters more
133	here than anywhere else.
134	
135	The same rule covers the analogical-transfer lens above and any idea resting on a claim
136	about how a real system works. A misremembered historical example carries the same risk as
137	an invented organism and reads just as confident. Phase 3 step 4 enforces this.
138	
139	Best for: efficiency, resilience, self-organisation, materials, distributed systems.
140	
141	### Morphological
142	
143	> List the 4-6 independent dimensions on which any solution must take a position (not
144	> features — dimensions, e.g. "who pays", "when value is delivered", "what is
145	> standardised"). For each, list 3-5 genuinely different options including at least one
146	> that no current player uses. Then — and this is the actual work — go through
147	> combinations and eliminate every pair of options that are mutually contradictory or
148	> jointly impossible. Report only the surviving combinations that are both internally
149	> consistent and unlike anything on the current market.
150	
151	**The pruning is the method.** Exhaustive enumeration collapses under combinatorial
152	explosion, and a model generates the grid so cheaply that it makes the volume problem
153	worse. A morphological pass without the cross-consistency prune is a machine for producing
154	filler. Short on budget? Skip this lens entirely rather than run it without the prune.
155	
156	Best for: business models, experimental design, many independent variables.
157	
158	### Actor reversal
159	
160	> List every actor in the system and what each currently gives and gets. Then
161	> systematically swap roles: the customer becomes the supplier, the regulator becomes the
162	> customer, the product becomes the distribution channel, the competitor becomes the
163	> infrastructure. For each swap that isn't absurd, describe what the business or system
164	> looks like from the other side.
165	
166	Best for: business-model problems, marketplaces, platform strategy, incumbent disruption.
167	
168	---
169	
170	## Demoted lenses
171	
172	Both are in wide use and neither survived the evidence review as a divergence tool. Kept
173	with narrowed scope rather than deleted, because each has one job it does well. Reasons in
174	`evidence.md`.
175	
176	### SCAMPER — iteration only, never a blank page
177	
178	Substitute / Combine / Adapt / Modify / Put to another use / Eliminate / Reverse.
179	
180	It's a checklist for transforming something that already exists, so it inherits that
181	thing's frame — which is why it didn't improve novelty in testing. Use it when the user has
182	a concrete artefact, process or product they want variations on; never to open a problem.
183	Eliminate and Reverse carry the weight; Modify reliably produces filler.
184	
185	### Six Thinking Hats — convergence only
186	
187	White facts / Red emotions / Black caution / Yellow optimism / Green creativity /
188	Blue process.
189	
190	The Green hat adds nothing a proper divergence phase doesn't do better. The Black hat is a
191	clean articulation of the one critique that's safe to run — what goes wrong, wh

Based on the research findings, here are the key causes for why engineers leave after 18 months of tenure:

## The Critical 18-Month Window

Engineers are most likely to leave between 18 and 24 months of tenure, at which point they have been at a company long enough to be fully productive and to understand the codebase and systems. This represents a turning point in their employment.

## Primary Reasons for Departure

Research identifies several key factors driving turnover:

1. **Lack of Meaningful Impact**: Engineers may spend extended periods building features that get shelved due to strategic pivots, leading to burnout from the feeling that their work doesn't matter.

2. **Management Issues**: Poor management drives 18% of departures, with data showing that people leave managers, not companies.

3. **Compensation and Career Growth**: Top reasons include compensation falling below market, no clear growth path or promotion clarity, poor manager relationships, and no real ownership or autonomy.

4. **Work Environment**: Meeting-heavy culture that blocks deep work, return-to-office mandates after remote work, and mission misalignment as the company scales are also significant factors.

5. **Burnout**: Research on software engineer burnout shows 43 percent more remote workers report working overtime than in-office teams.

## Important Context

Compensation alone rarely causes engineers to leave—it's usually two or more of these factors stacking. The departure at 18 months appears to be driven by a combination of factors that accumulate as engineers become more fully aware of their work environment and career trajectory.

I've performed a web search on senior software engineer retention strategies for startups losing engineers to big tech. Here are the key findings:

## Why Senior Engineers Leave Startups

If you're losing senior engineers, compensation is rarely the actual cause—even when stated as such. The three real drivers are manager quality, scope decay, and AI fatigue. Senior developers don't quit because they hate coding; they quit because they're treated like implementers, not architects.

## Core Retention Strategies

**Autonomy and Trust:** 48% of engineers leave due to micromanagement. Senior engineers need the freedom to make architectural decisions without constant oversight. Forcing them to justify every choice to non-technical leaders sends the message that you don't trust them.

**Challenging, Meaningful Work:** Companies offering variety—new tech stacks, cross-functional projects, and innovation sprints—retain higher engagement rates, and developers with access to cutting-edge technologies are 48% less likely to leave within a year.

**Career Growth:** Companies offering career development see 2.9x better retention. If the ratio of Director-and-above to Staff-and-above is more than 3:1, your IC ladder is functionally a dead end—and your most technical senior engineers know it.

**Maker Time:** Senior engineers can drift into 25 meetings a week without shipping anything substantive. Companies that make a 60% maker-time policy explicit for Staff+ engineers, like Stripe and Linear, have the strongest senior engineer retention.

**Mission Alignment:** When pivots are necessary, involve senior engineers in the reasoning. Engineers who understand the "why" behind strategic changes are far more likely to re-commit than those who feel the rug was pulled.

I found comprehensive information on the topics you searched for. Here's a summary of the key findings:

## Standard Vesting Structure

The four-year vesting schedule with a one-year cliff is widely regarded as the standard for startup equity, with 90% of private companies sticking to this structure. The standard approach uses a 4-year vesting period with a 1-year cliff: 25% vest after year one, with the remaining 75% vesting monthly thereafter.

## The Retention Cliff Problem

When an early employee fully vests after 4 years, their financial incentive to stay essentially disappears. This is called a retention cliff, and it tends to hit right when your most experienced people have the least reason to stay.

## Equity Refresh Grants

A refresh grant (or refresher) is a new equity grant given to existing employees, typically once a year after the first year. Refreshers were created to address the 'vesting cliff' problem: as your original grant vests, your remaining unvested equity goes down, reducing your retention incentive. A refresh grant resets that incentive by adding new unvested equity.

At Series A, a simple policy is: employees who hit their two-year anniversary receive a refresh grant equal to 25% of their initial grant, vesting over four years. This Wealthfront-style model requires minimal administration and prevents the retention cliff at year three.

## Refresh Grants and Counteroffers

Most startups do not have formal refresh programs and only give new equity at significant life events: promotion, hitting a major retention milestone, or as part of a counter-offer when you have another offer in hand.

I found comprehensive information on stay interviews, alumni networks, boomerang employees, and retention programs. Here are the key findings:

## Boomerang Employee Benefits

Rehiring alumni saves about $50,000 per hire. More significantly, boomerang employees stay 44% longer over three years compared to new hires. Boomerangs reach productivity faster, stay longer, and cost less to source than external hires – up to 50% reduction in cost-per-hire and 44% higher three-year retention.

## Alumni Network Programs

P&G, HSBC, Nestle, Accenture, and McKinsey run successful alumni programs. Sodexo's U.S. alumni network includes nearly 9,000 management-level employees with about 20% of external hires annually from former employees, while Deloitte's U.S. network has grown to 200,000 people with 2,800 boomerang employees returning in one fiscal year—32% more than the previous period.

## Stay Interviews and Exit Conversations

Exit interviews should include questions that look forward, like asking what would motivate departing employees to return and discussing skills they hope to develop externally. The key lies in transforming exit interviews into "future opportunity conversations" and developing specific recruitment pathways for returning talent.

## Re-onboarding Strategies

A boomerang employee's return requires a specific process distinct from standard onboarding, with adapted re-onboarding recognizing both the employee's familiarity and changes during their absence. When an alumnus signals interest in returning, the process is expedited with a lighter interview panel focused on what changed since they left and accelerated onboarding.

## Maintaining Alumni Engagement

Simple, consistent actions like newsletters or LinkedIn messages can maintain relationships with former employees, while invitations to company events or training sessions provide additional touchpoints without requiring heavy resources.

7	  {"id": "p1-005", "text": "Publish a standing price at which any employer may buy out a departing specialist's deferred claim, split the fee with the person, and run departures as football-style transfers."},
8	  {"id": "p1-006", "text": "Grant a standing right to take an outside job for up to two years and return to the same seat with tenure, stake and vesting clock unbroken, exercisable once."},
9	  {"id": "p1-007", "text": "Employ specialists three days a week and formally bless the other two for anyone else, so an outside offer forecloses nothing and there is no whole thing to leave."},
10	  {"id": "p1-008", "text": "Give a seven-year employment guarantee with an escalating severance floor, contractually binding the firm and not the person, renewed to seven years every anniversary."},
11	  {"id": "p1-009", "text": "Grant the full equity package at hire subject to a clawback that shrinks to zero over eight years, so the person is always wealthier by staying one more year rather than poorer by leaving."},
12	  {"id": "p1-010", "text": "Fund the specialist's own company as a subsidiary, take a minority stake, and let them run it as founder while remaining on payroll."},
13	  {"id": "p1-011", "text": "Contractually route inbound recruiter offers through the firm, pay a bounty for each forwarded, and commit to matching or beating by published formula within seventy-two hours."},
14	  {"id": "p1-012", "text": "Choose only projects whose feedback loop is longer than five years — regulatory, materials, longitudinal, physical — so nobody is fully effective at twelve months and the capability curve never flattens."},
15	  {"id": "p1-013", "text": "Pay part of compensation as a decade-long, personally directed research budget with guaranteed compute and lab time, drawable only while employed and never transferable."},
16	  {"id": "p1-014", "text": "Have the specialist hold copyright to what they write and license it to the firm on an annually renewing fee that escalates with tenure."},
17	  {"id": "p1-015", "text": "Stagger many small unvested claims at irregular dates set by project events rather than anniversaries, so no clean exit window ever opens."},
18	  {"id": "p1-016", "text": "Give each specialist an operating role in one internal venture plus board seats in three others, so their market-value peaks arrive staggered and none coincide."},
19	  {"id": "p1-017", "text": "Reset every person's pay to the highest verified outside offer received by anyone at their level in the firm that quarter, and post the number internally."},
20	  {"id": "p1-018", "text": "Make the person co-owner of the customer relationship with a contractual revenue share on named accounts that survives only under this firm's paper."},
21	  {"id": "p1-019", "text": "Cap total headcount by charter so ownership fractions can only concentrate, and publish each person's percentage and how it rises when others leave."},
22	  {"id": "p1-020", "text": "Domicile a public institution — a standards body, conference or journal — inside the firm and appoint the specialist its chair, funded and staffed."},
23	  {"id": "p1-021", "text": "When a large employer makes an offer, bid to acquire the project or team they wanted the person for, and give the person that mandate here."},
24	  {"id": "p1-022", "text": "Pay the first eight weeks entirely for writing the ramp path and tooling for their own role, so full effectiveness arrives at month three and the twelve-month clock never sets the rhythm."},
25	  {"id": "p1-023", "text": "Carry a below-market mortgage or housing loan on the firm's balance sheet that converts to an outright grant at year six."},
26	  {"id": "p1-024", "text": "Ship all significant work under a permanent two-person signature, assigning every specialist a fixed dyad partner, so the legible public artifact names a pair and not an individual."},
27	  {"id": "p1-025", "text": "Replace the fixed-term contract with a rolling multi-year agreement that auto-extends every quarter, so remaining requires no decision and leaving requires an affirmative one."},
28	  {"id": "p1-026", "text": "Keep a longitudinal instrumented record of each person's own decisions and outcomes over years, feed it back to them privately, and let them take a copy only on ten-year tenure."},
29	  {"id": "p1-027", "text": "Require every specialist to automate their previous job before starting the next one, and pay a bonus scaled to how much of their old role the machine now performs."},
30	  {"id": "p1-028", "text": "Underwrite the person's income against their own risk-taking: guarantee five years of pay at current level if a bet they personally chose fails publicly."},
31	  {"id": "p1-029", "text": "Write a dated, funded ten-year plan per person with capital committed at each milestone in advance, so the horizon on offer always exceeds any outside offer's horizon."},
32	  {"id": "p1-030", "text": "Sell a minority of each specialist's future firm-linked upside back to them for cash at hire, so they hold a bought asset rather than a granted one and would be selling, not quitting."}
33	 ]}
